newsitem.title: UK: UK's Labour party history rooted in trade unionism.
newsitem.headline: UK's Labour party history rooted in trade unionism.

text.p: Britain's Labour Party was founded by trade unionists at the end of the nineteenth century and the links between the two arms of the labour movement -- cultural, financial, institutional -- have remained strong ever since.
An Act of 1871 formally recognised trade unions but left them open to prosecution if they tried actively to further their interests, for example by picketing.
The Trades Union Congress umbrella body thus decided to form a "Parliamentary Committee" to lobby for a change to the laws.
In 1892, 10 trade unionists were elected to parliament on a Liberal ticket, and three others were elected as independents.

In 1900, a special conference called by the Parliamentary Committee voted to set up a Labour Representation Committee. In the 1906 election, 29 Committee supporters were voted into parliament, and the Committee became the Labour Party.
By 1924 there was a Labour Prime Minister, Ramsay MacDonald leading the country for a few months with Liberal support. A second Labour government was in power from 1929-1931.
Present Labour leader Tony Blair has cut union influence while moving the party to the political centre, attracting funds from business, lobby groups and rich individuals along the way.
But for the time being Labour still needs union money.
According to the party's accounts, its 1995 income totalled 15.07 million pounds, including 2.56 million which went into a specific general election campaign fund.
Some 6.8 million of that total came from fees from affiliated groups, the bulk of it from trade unions.
The Transport and General Workers Union (T&G) gave Labour around 1.25 million pounds in affiliation fees and other donations in 1995 and the GMB general union 1.4 million.

Until last year, unions also sponsored individual Labour Members of Parliament (MPs), providing money for their constituency and research work.In 1995, the T&G sponsored 38 Labour MPs of all political hues, including Blair.
The party has now asked that this money be redirected to help Labour's election campaign in marginal constituencies.
In the past, the unions wielded power within the party commensurate with their financial contribution.

Even in 1995, they commanded 70 percent of the vote at Labour's annual conference. This year it is down to 50 percent -- ordinary constituency members have the rest -- and Blair is likely to ignore conference votes that go against him.
The reduction in the union vote was negotiated by Blair as party membership rose. It stands at about 400,000 now, up from 365,000 at end-1995 and about 275,000 at the 1992 election.
The unions have a third of the votes in the college that chooses the party leader, with MPs and constituency members also having a third each. Blair was elected by this method in 1994.
The unions have also accepted "one-member one-vote" in constituency ballots for election candidates, giving up the block votes formerly wielded by union delegates.
But union representatives still fill 12 of the 29 seats on the party's ruling national executive, and -- not unnaturally -- other seats can be filled by people with a union background.
General secretary Tom Sawyer was previously deputy leader of public services trade union Unison, Britain's biggest.
All the same, there seems little chance of any of the present crop of union leaders making it into a Blair cabinet.
It was different in the old days.
In 1940, Winston Churchill made Ernest Bevin, the leader of the T&G, Minister of Labour in his wartime cabinet. When Labour swept to power after the war, Bevin became Foreign Secretary.

In 1964, under Labour premier Harold Wilson, Frank Cousins briefly swapped his job at the top of the T&G for that of Minister of Technology and Ray Gunter, formerly of the Transport Salaried Staffs Association, became Minister of Labour.
Gunter later resigned from the cabinet, complaining that it was "overweighted with intellectuals".
